rule: A skill directory requires a `SKILL.md`; `scripts/`, `references/` and `assets/` are optional. This comes from an open specification.

The file must be named exactly `SKILL.md` (case-sensitive), the folder name must be kebab-case, and the skill folder must not contain a `README.md`. The source is a guide dated January 2026 that has not been checked against the current version, and the README rule is absent from the open specification.

`name` is 1-64 characters of a-z, 0-9 and hyphens; it "Must not start or end with a hyphen", has no `--`, and "Must match the parent directory name". Whether the field is mandatory or optional differs between sources.
`description` is 1-1024 characters and "Should describe both what the skill does and when to use it".

The description is a trigger condition, not a summary: "the description field is not a summary, it's a description of when to trigger this skill"; "the description carries the entire burden of triggering". One of the supporting sources is secondary.
Open point: whether the description should be written in third person or as an imperative ("Use this skill when...") is not settled; sources differ.
Avoid generic skill names such as `helper`, `utils`, `tools`, `documents`, `data`, `files`, and vague descriptions such as "Helps with documents".
Description plus `when_to_use` is truncated at 1,536 characters in Claude Code, so "Put the key use case first". This reflects the docs as read on 2026-11-04.

In Claude Code the skill listing budget is 1% of the context window; rarely invoked skills lose their descriptions; check with `/doctor`; `skillOverrides` supports `name-only`; `skillListingBudgetFraction` raises the budget.
Do not use `<` or `>` (XML tags) in frontmatter, because frontmatter sits in the system prompt and hostile content could inject instructions. The source is a guide dated January 2026.
Open point: whether skill names that contain or start with "claude" or "anthropic" are reserved. The same guide says "in name" on one page and "prefix" on another.
Keep the `SKILL.md` body under 500 lines.
Keep the body under about 5,000 tokens ("< 5000 tokens recommended"). The number is stated, but the unit differs across sources (tokens versus words), so the unit is open.
Use three-level progressive disclosure: frontmatter is always loaded, the body loads when relevant, linked files load when needed; "keep the core of the skill lean".
Reference files one level deep from `SKILL.md`: "Keep references one level deep from `SKILL.md`." Reason: Claude may only run `head -100` on nested files.
Write only what Claude does not already know: "Only add context Claude doesn't already have."; test each line with "Would the agent get this wrong without this instruction?"
Put a Gotchas section in `SKILL.md`: "The highest-value content in many skills is a list of gotchas"; each time the agent has to be corrected, add the fix to Gotchas.

A rule that must hold every time belongs in a hook or script, not only in prose: "Claude Code runs a hook every time its event occurs ... whether or not Claude is following the skill"; "Code is deterministic; language interpretation isn't."; a skill is only "a control, though an advisory one".

Put the most important instructions at the top of `SKILL.md`, because after compaction the end of a skill body is cut ("Truncation keeps the start of the file"). Claude Code; figures as documented on 2026-11-04.

Write guidance that applies to a whole task as standing instructions: "Claude Code does not re-read the skill file on later turns, so write guidance that should apply throughout a task as standing instructions rather than one-time steps." Claude Code.
Match specificity to how fragile the task is: "Match the level of specificity to the task's fragility and variability."; "Calibrate each part independently."
Explain the reason instead of issuing rigid directives: "explaining why can be more effective than rigid directives"; ALWAYS/NEVER commands persuade less than reasoning.
Give defaults, not menus ("Provide defaults, not menus"), and prefer procedures over declarations.
Use one consistent term throughout, and do not write information that will go stale (use an "Old patterns" section instead).
One job per skill: a skill that tries to do too much will "straddle several and confuse the agent". The source is secondary.
Validate the format with tools: `skills-ref validate ./my-skill` and `claude plugin validate`. `claude plugin validate` needs Claude Code v2.1.233 or later.
Install skills only from trusted sources.
`allowed-tools` in frontmatter does not narrow the tool set; prefer narrow patterns over a bare `Bash`. This rests on a single course source and the field is not in one guide's frontmatter list.

A skill that need not trigger itself should be manual-only (`disable-model-invocation: true` keeps its description out of context). Claude Code; the mechanism is stated, turning it into a rule is inferred.

Invocation-graph constraint: a user-invoked skill may call a model-invoked skill but not another user-invoked skill. The source is a community repository, not the vendor, and checking it by machine is inferred.

Attach only the skills each agent needs; at most 500 skills per session; repo skills must sit at `.claude/skills/<name>/SKILL.md`, one level deep. This is from a beta managed-agents product; only the shape is borrowed for local harnesses.
Open point: ownership and lifecycle of a large skill set (owner, retirement, versions) has no source.
Keep `CLAUDE.md` under 200 lines: "Keep CLAUDE.md under 200 lines, give it an owner, and review changes to it like code." The source speaks only about `CLAUDE.md`.

Open point: whether the 200-line limit also applies to other markdown (role profiles, handoff notes) and to profiles loaded through `systemPrompt`. No source measures an optimal length outside `CLAUDE.md`.
`@import` helps organize but does not cut context cost: "Imports help you organize a long file but don't reduce its context cost".
Write down only what Claude cannot find in the repo: "Only write down what Claude can't find by reading the repo, or what it would otherwise spend time rediscovering every session."
Write instructions that are specific and verifiable ("Use 2-space indentation" rather than "Format code properly"), and make sure they do not contradict each other. `/doctor prompt-audit` can help.
`CLAUDE.md` guides but does not enforce: "`CLAUDE.md` is for guidelines, and Claude is allowed to decide a guideline doesn't apply." A "never" rule belongs in a deny rule or hook.
If a line is still missed after adding emphasis, it belongs in a hook; heavy emphasis makes Claude over-apply the rule.

In Claude Code, rules with `paths:` and subdirectory `CLAUDE.md` files live in the conversation and are lost to summarization on compaction; a rule that must survive should drop `paths:` or go in the root `CLAUDE.md`.
A rule without `paths:` is the same as putting the content in `CLAUDE.md`: "always loaded, always costing tokens".
Use a rule with `paths:` when a convention applies to files scattered across the codebase (instead of a subdirectory `CLAUDE.md`).
Multi-step procedures, or content relevant to only part of the codebase, move to a skill or a path-scoped rule; reference material goes to a skill.
In Claude Code, editing `CLAUDE.md` mid-session does not take effect until `/clear`, `/compact` or a restart. The event is stated; the edit procedure that records reloading the session is inferred.
In Claude Code, block-level HTML comments in `CLAUDE.md` are stripped before entering context, so they can hold maintainer notes.
Record repeated mistakes in `CLAUDE.md`: "A repeated mistake or a recurring review comment is a CLAUDE.md edit"; "Anything you've had to correct twice already".
Commit the file to git, give it an owner, and review changes like code.
Keep it under one page with four sections (Commands, Conventions, Architecture, Things Claude gets wrong). The source is a course, so it is secondary.
Add a section telling compaction what to preserve ("include a section telling it what to preserve when summarizing"); durable rules go in `CLAUDE.md` because it is reloaded on every request.
`CLAUDE.md` is layered: personal (`$HOME/.claude/CLAUDE.md`, not shared through git), project, and directory levels add up; skills and subagents of the same name override instead.
Position matters: put key findings summaries at the start of aggregated input and give details clear headings ("lost in the middle").
Progressive summarization loses figures, dates and expectations; keep a "case facts" block outside the summarized history, and record source and date when sources conflict.

Treat `CLAUDE.md`, `AGENTS.md` and notes written by outsiders or other agents as potentially untrusted input; shared memory should be mounted read-only when writing is not needed. The stated source is a beta managed-agents product; applying it to handoff files is inferred.
If a repo has `AGENTS.md`, Claude Code can read it instead of `CLAUDE.md`; use `@AGENTS.md` to share one file.

Choose where content lives: `CLAUDE.md` is always loaded; skills load on demand; hooks run per event; subagents have their own context; a hook's context cost is "Zero, unless the hook returns output".

One role per file: frontmatter (name, model, tools) plus a body that is the system prompt; keep the role prompt separate from task instructions ("The system prompt is distinct from user messages, which should describe the work to be done."). The shape comes from a beta product; applying it to local harnesses is inferred.
An orchestrator prompt states goals and quality criteria rather than listing every step.

Each delegation to a subagent needs an objective, output format, guidance on tools and sources, and task boundaries: "Without detailed task descriptions, agents duplicate work, leave gaps, or fail to find necessary information."

Pass subagent context explicitly in the prompt: "The only content you pass from parent to subagent is the Agent tool's prompt string"; a subagent "doesn't see your conversation history". A fork inherits everything; an ordinary subagent does not.
A subagent description should single out one role ("Write descriptions that single out one subagent").
Use explicit criteria rather than general advice: "be conservative" or "only report high-confidence findings" do not improve precision. Context: code review.
Use 2-4 few-shot examples for ambiguous cases, with the reason for choosing each; give concrete input/output examples when verbal descriptions are read inconsistently.
Aim for a moderate altitude: start from a minimal prompt and add instructions based on observed failures.

With newer models use plain wording and drop heavy emphasis and old instructions: "piling on emphasis mostly makes Claude over-apply the rule"; "these models might now overtrigger. The fix is to soften any aggressive language." Model dependent; an instruction to "use a subagent to check" is a related open point.

State when delegation to a subagent or workflow is allowed, or set a hard cap: "give explicit guidance on which scenarios warrant delegation, or set deterministic caps on how many agents can be launched".
State in the prompt that content from tools, documents and searches is untrusted data and must not override the original instructions. The source speaks about the `tool_result` API.

Do not put user text inside a `tool_result` block; harness text inserted after a tool result is sparse and separate from the user's words. Applying this to `PostToolUse` hooks or relays is inferred and needs testing.
Hard length limits in a prompt can reduce work quality; a model-specific change must be pinned to its target model.
Each role has a stop condition and reports when blocked or when the task is impossible, instead of working around it. Evidence is from internal model behavior; applying it to a harness is inference.
Keep the initializer prompt and the continuation prompt in two separate files. The source is a demo, not a production recommendation.
A reminder against "laziness" is more effective in the user prompt than in `SKILL.md`. The source gives one sentence and no data.
Sensitive keywords in a system prompt can create unintended tool associations.
When several teams each add one sentence to a system prompt, contradictory rules result (a "Frankenprompt").
Declare model and effort explicitly in the role profile (or use `inherit` deliberately), because defaults depend on version and environment variables. Inferred.

A reviewer states alternatives before recommending; the human states an opinion before seeing the agent's proposal. Inferred from an experiment on causal analysis; the source measured the effect and wrote no rule.
Open point: whether long instructions on tool usage belong in the system prompt or in the tool description.
Open point: multi-phase role profiles (phases plus a supervisor role) have no source.

What must happen without exception should be enforced by a mechanism (a `command` or `http` hook, a deny rule, a managed setting, `tools:`), not by instruction: "If something has to happen every time, make it a hook, a deny rule, or a managed setting."

`prompt` and `agent` hooks are not deterministic; for real enforcement use `command` or `http` with `onFailure: "block"`. `onFailure` needs Claude Code v2.1.295 or later and `agent` hooks are experimental.

A policy hook blocks with `exit 2`; "Exit code 1 without valid JSON output is a non-blocking error"; "Exit 2 blocks even when your hook prints JSON". The table of events that can block is a condensed copy and needs checking against the original.
Hooks fail open by default: "On most events, when a hook fails or times out, Claude Code still carries out the action"; `Stop`, `SubagentStop`, `TaskCompleted` and `TeammateIdle` ignore `onFailure`.
Open point: whether a timed-out `PreToolUse` hook blocks the tool call.

A `PreToolUse` `deny` holds even under `bypassPermissions` or `--dangerously-skip-permissions`; an `allow` hook cannot override a `deny` rule; hooks run before every step. Not yet run on a local Claude Code.
Hard blocks by name or path go in permission rules first; hooks handle dynamic logic: "use the permission system rather than a hook to enforce a hard allow or deny".

A matcher matches only the tool name, so a hook that guards file writes must cover both `Bash` and the file-writing tools, or it can be bypassed with `echo > file`. The matcher behavior is stated; the protection scope is inferred.
On a `Stop` hook, check `stop_hook_active`; after 8 consecutive blocks with no tool call Claude Code stops blocking by itself. `CLAUDE_CODE_STOP_HOOK_BLOCK_CAP` raises the cap.
Hook scripts: output from the shell profile (`.zshrc`) on stdout corrupts JSON; use absolute paths or `${CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR}`.
Hooks merge across settings levels; managed hooks cannot be disabled; `allowManagedHooksOnly` blocks outside hooks.
Hooks and plugins run code with the user's rights ("what the plugin runs, it runs as you"), so review them like code. The rights are stated; the review rule is inferred.

Treat mods and channels as "not adopted": mods are not sandboxed and can approve tool calls before asking; channels let people reply to the tool-approval channel. Mods need v2.1.287 or later; channels are a research preview. The risks are stated; the advice to skip them is inferred.
Permission order: "Rules are evaluated in order: deny, then ask, then allow."; "An allow rule can't carve an exception out of a deny rule."; a deny at any level wins; managed settings are highest.
`allowed_tools` does not constrain `bypassPermissions`; to block, use `disallowed_tools` or a hook. SDK; the `default` mode denies calls that need approval from Claude Code v2.1.302.
Removing a tool is stronger than blocking by pattern: `disallowed_tools=["Bash"]` drops the definition from the request, while `Bash(rm *)` blocks only that pattern.

The sandbox covers shell only: "The sandbox covers shell commands only. Claude's file tools, MCP servers, and hooks run outside it."; it is off by default; `denyRead` does not block the Read tool and `allowedDomains` does not limit WebFetch. An older source differs, so prefer the newer; the "Security limitations" section was not read.
Unattended roles: enable the sandbox with `allowUnsandboxedCommands: false` and `failIfUnavailable: true`. Inferred.
Use `dontAsk` with a narrow allow list for locked-down agents: "For a locked-down agent, pair `allowedTools` with `permissionMode: "dontAsk"`".

Use `bypassPermissions` only in a container or VM without internet; auto mode "does not guarantee safety", 17% of overeager actions are missed, and it is "not a drop-in replacement for careful human review on high-stakes infrastructure". Figures are vendor-internal and not reproduced.
The `permissionMode` in subagent frontmatter is ignored when the main session runs in `bypassPermissions`, `acceptEdits` or auto mode.
Hard constraints belong in managed settings or deny rules, not in allow rules or subagent frontmatter. Inferred.
Restrict subagents with `tools:` or `disallowedTools:`; `Agent(worker, researcher)` limits which subagents may be spawned; a removed tool "isn't in the subagent's session at all".

Hard caps for an agent tree: default depth 3, default concurrency 20, `maxBudgetUsd` returns `Budget limit reached`; one workflow may run at most 1,000 agents. The numbers come from the docs and were not run.

Set `max_turns` and `max_budget_usd` for production agents; hitting a cap returns `error_max_turns` or `error_max_budget_usd` with no `result`; the budget is soft (overshoot by at most one response): "Leave headroom for this". A budget that covers subagents needs Claude Code v2.1.217+; `maxTurns` on a subagent returns "partial" from v2.1.246.
Open point: per-role cap values (turn counts, money) have no source.

Subagent model order: call parameter, then `model` in frontmatter, then `CLAUDE_CODE_SUBAGENT_MODEL`, then the main model; `CLAUDE_CODE_SUBAGENT_MODEL_FORCE=1` forces all. The order changed in v2.1.251, so record the version.

Effort order: `CLAUDE_CODE_EFFORT_LEVEL`, then the in-session choice, then `--effort`, then settings, then the model default; a subagent's `effort` frontmatter does not override the environment variable.
Environment variables that force model or effort silently disable role profiles; check for them. Inferred.
Open point: the default effort of the Sonnet 5.5 model is not settled by the sources.
Configuration defaults (effort, caching, prompt limits) are quality choices; review changes like code.
Changing model, effort, or the MCP/tool set mid-session loses the cache; pick model and effort at session start and compact at task boundaries. Claude Code; do not hard-code TTL or price figures.
MCP scopes: project `.mcp.json` (shared via git, needs approval on use) and personal `$HOME/.claude.json`; secrets go through `${GITHUB_TOKEN}` and are not committed.
MCP config precedence: local, project, user, plugin, connector; "The entire server entry from that source is used; fields are not merged across scopes."
Connect only trusted MCP servers (prompt injection risk); `headersHelper` runs arbitrary shell commands once the directory is trusted.
Keep secrets outside the agent boundary: an external proxy injects keys; do not put the Claude API key in the sandbox; keep URLs separate from tokens.
Isolate several agents on one machine with their own `cwd`, `settingSources: []`, `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR`, and shared auto memory turned off. SDK.
Use structured telemetry without content (`OTEL_LOG_USER_PROMPTS` and `OTEL_LOG_TOOL_CONTENT` are off by default); assign identity per role. Traces are beta.

Deny by default; version and review configuration; test rollback; write the allowed and forbidden policy down (Foundation level). One PDF source could not be read and the Enterprise level is unchecked.
Match isolation to the capacity for oversight: "Match isolation strength to the user's capacity for oversight." The principle is stated; that background roles need harder boundaries is inferred.
Skills from a repo are a trust boundary: anyone who can commit to the repo can add a skill and the platform loads it without a review step. Beta managed-agents product.
Open point: whether hooks and `settings` take effect in sessions opened by a launcher or agent-hosting platform rather than the vendor CLI directly.
Hand off with structure to a person who cannot see the transcript. The original example is a customer-support escalation.
A fresh session with a structured summary is more reliable than a resume that carries old tool results.

Keep state in files: an initializer run first, a progress file (`claude-progress.txt`), a feature list and descriptive git commits; end with the environment "in a clean state". The reference is demo code.
Store state data as JSON and progress notes as text; models are less likely to corrupt JSON than Markdown.
The feature list may only change the `passes` field; "It is unacceptable to remove or edit tests".
At session start read the git log and progress notes, pick the highest-priority unfinished item, and run verification before new work.
One task per session; end cleanly (commit, update progress, leave the application runnable).
Agree on "done" before writing code (a sprint contract between generator and evaluator).

Separate the grader from the worker: "agents reliably skew positive when grading their own work" (stated for subjective tasks) and "even on tasks that do have verifiable outcomes, agents still sometimes exhibit poor judgment"; "completion is decided by a fresh model rather than the one doing the work"; "The grader uses a separate context window". Quote with its context.

A completion condition is a measurable end state, how to prove it, and constraints that must not change; at most 4,000 characters; the evaluator sees only Claude's output. For `/goal`, retry (three times then pause) applies only to interactive sessions from v2.1.269; check-ins need v2.1.236 and are capped at three from v2.1.246.

A rubric lists criteria that can be graded one by one ("The CSV contains a price column with numeric values" instead of "The data looks good"); "vague criteria produce noisy evaluations". Beta managed-agents product.

Put the "is it really done" gate at `SubagentStop`, `TaskCompleted`, `TeammateIdle` or `Stop` (exit 2 keeps the work going); check `stop_hook_active`. These events ignore `onFailure: "block"`. Inferred.
Do not treat passing tests as done; the verifier must be nearly perfect, or the agent solves the wrong problem: "the task verifier is nearly perfect, otherwise Claude will solve the wrong problem".
Split a large review into a local per-file pass and a cross-file integration pass; when re-running a review, put earlier findings in context and report only what is new or unaddressed.

Review in tiers; review level follows the risk of the change, not the author; an approval is tied to one commit; an agent's approval does not replace a human's; "Whoever prompted the change is on the hook for it." The source is secondary and the tier thresholds are not published.
Cap review rounds: after three rounds the reviewer asks the author to rethink the approach; re-review covers the diff only and flags error classes instead of single lines.

A human reviewer is an independent check only when the judgment is their own: "a human reviewer is only an independent check if their judgment is their own". Recording whether a proposal came from a person or an agent is inferred.

A message between agents is not user consent and cannot change configuration: "a message from another session never counts as your consent". Agent teams are experimental; platforms that host agents outside the vendor product do not get these guarantees automatically.
The `auto` mode of a managed-agents product is not a human checkpoint; work that needs human approval should use `always_ask`. Beta; the name clashes with the auto mode of Claude Code.
A pull request is a checkpoint; the agent that wrote the code cannot approve it: "Separation of duties is preserved, because the agent that wrote the code has no way to approve it."

Use multiple agents only when needed: "Start with the simplest approach that works, and add complexity only when evidence supports it."; cost is about 15 times the tokens of chat in one source or 3-10 times in another; "Outside these situations, the coordination costs typically exceed the benefits." One source has no verbatim "start with a single agent".
Divide work along context boundaries (the agent that builds a feature also writes its tests); beware the "telephone game" that degrades fidelity at handoff; subagents should return light references.

A handoff contract is verified: the input schema is checked "before any application side effects", the context passed on is filtered, and the output is an artifact with an identity. Each element comes from a different non-vendor source; combining them into a pattern is inferred.
When agents share a filesystem but keep separate contexts, hand off through files, not memory. Beta platform; inferred.

Unattended runs: read from a bookmark; report an unreadable source rather than treating it as quiet; confirm before writing state, and write "maybe posted" if unsure; read-only access and a cost cap per run. Beta, secondary source, about chat and code-hosting integrations.
Compact at task boundaries, `/clear` between unrelated tasks, and delegate large reads to subagents.
Use plan mode for large changes with several valid directions or many files.

Revisit harness assumptions when the model changes: "every component in a harness encodes an assumption about what the model can't do on its own"; "those assumptions need to be frequently questioned because they can go stale as models improve".
A change that may trade away quality needs a soak period, a broad eval and a gradual rollout; dogfood with the exact public build. No soak threshold is given.
Keep a dated change log of the harness so quality drops can be correlated (the "missed correlation" lesson). Inferred.
Isolate untrusted content: a reading agent without privileges, an acting agent that sees only a summary; separate reading from acting.
Adversarial verification of each subagent output against a rubric; but "most traditional coding tasks do not need a panel of 5 reviewers". Secondary source.
Loop stop conditions: "it's also common to include stopping conditions (such as a maximum number of iterations) to maintain control". The source says "common", not mandatory.
Open point: a process-level decision record (who decided what, why, evidence, result) for unattended sessions has no source.
Open point: gated phases and a supervisor role have no source.
A tool description is the main factor: "Provide extremely detailed descriptions. This is by far the most important factor in tool performance."
A description states what the tool does, when to use it and when not, the meaning of each parameter, and limits; at least 3-4 sentences.
State input formats, example queries, edge cases and boundaries; rename and re-describe tools to remove overlap.

Each tool has one distinct purpose and there are few tools: "Make sure each tool you build has a clear, distinct purpose."; yet also "Consolidate related operations into fewer tools". Open point: where the line between merging and splitting sits.
Tool names carry a service or resource prefix and match `^[a-zA-Z0-9_-]{1,128}$`; a full MCP tool name is `mcp__{server}__{tool}`.
Return only high-signal output with stable, meaningful identifiers (slug or UUID); long responses waste context. One source prefers natural-language names, another accepts slugs or UUIDs.
Claude Code's default output limit is 25,000 tokens with a warning above 10,000 (`MAX_MCP_OUTPUT_TOKENS` changes it); when truncating, tell the agent how to narrow (pagination, ranges, filters).
An error says what went wrong and what to try next; MCP sets `isError: true`, the API sets `is_error: true`; an uncaught exception is turned into a raw error.
Distinguish an access error from a valid empty result; do not swallow errors as success.

Tolerate call differences: accept case differences when matching is unambiguous, or return `is_error: true` with the correct name; "Change the arguments so that it is harder to make mistakes." Applying this to CLIs is inferred.
Annotations (`readOnlyHint` and others) are metadata, not enforcement: "A tool marked `readOnlyHint: true` can still write to disk"; keep them true to the handler.
`allowed_callers` is not a security boundary. API.

Too many tools reduce selection reliability (for example 18 versus 4-5); load on demand (tool search, `alwaysLoad` only for the few tools used every turn). The tool-search threshold is not consistent across sources.
For MCP descriptions and instructions put key details and keywords first; they are cut at 4,096 characters (preloaded) or 16,384 (via tool search). Claude Code docs of 2026-11-04.
Tools that write files must guard against directory traversal.
Tool results are untrusted content: keep them in `tool_result` and verify before trusting.
Use a narrow custom tool so the server keeps the final decision ("Give the agent one narrow custom tool").
Tools should be self-contained, robust to errors and clear in purpose; avoid bloated toolsets.
Do not add a tool just to "think"; the vendor recommends extended thinking instead of the think tool (updated 2025-12-15). The quote is not verbatim.
Prefer an existing MCP server for standard integrations; write your own only for custom workflows.
CLI for CI: `-p`/`--print` (non-interactive), `--output-format json`, `--json-schema`.
Prefer CLI tools over MCP when available (saves tokens): "Prefer CLI tools when available". The source is a single line.
A programmable interface (an API or CLI with machine-readable output) beats an operation that needs full local state. Inferred from large-scale infrastructure that does not apply directly.
Open point: designing a CLI for agents (exit codes, flags, output format, error messages) has no source.
Keep a manual-run script for trial and a record of every run; stop cleanly with SIGTERM and wait before a hard kill. Stated for a cloud/beta context; applying it to harness CLIs is inferred.
A hook that logs every tool call with the session ID is the minimum audit trail. Inferred.
Separate regression evals (near 100% pass) from capability evals (start at a low pass rate); run regression on every agent or model change. Applying this to a multi-agent harness is inferred.
Start with 20-50 tasks taken from real failures; balance cases that should and should not act: "One-sided evals create one-sided optimization."
A good task is one where two independent experts reach the same pass/fail verdict; 0% pass across many runs usually means a broken task.
Grade the product, not the path; allow partial credit; guard against graders being gamed; start every run from a clean environment.
Run several trials because output varies; use pass^k for agents that must be consistent. The number of trials for a harness is an open point.
Use deterministic graders where possible and LLM graders where needed; an LLM judge has an "Unknown" exit, is calibrated against humans, and is not the model under test. One source is secondary.
Read transcripts and execution traces, not only final results: "Read agent execution traces, not just final outputs."

Know the measurement noise before trusting a change: a gap under about 3 points is suspect; record the run environment configuration with results. The 3-point figure is from one benchmark, not from any specific harness.
Split train and test; do not paste failures into the prompt; change one thing at a time; revert if train rises while test stays flat; do not merge if within noise. Secondary source.
Keep answers and grading criteria out of the agent's reach; treat eval integrity as a continuing adversarial problem. The source concerns a web benchmark; applying it to a harness folder is inferred.
An eval at 100% only tracks regression and gives no improvement signal; review periodically; do not trust a score before reading the details.
Run evals when `CLAUDE.md`, skills or hooks change; gate configuration changes on the results; write one eval case per incident, owned by the team. Course and blog sources.
A one-line prompt or default change needs a broad per-model eval and per-line ablation; code review, unit tests, end-to-end tests and dogfooding do not prove there is no regression.
An eval must tell a correct version from a wrong one; monitor quality continuously in the real environment.

Skill trigger test: about 20 queries (8-10 of each kind, including near-misses), run 3 times, threshold 0.5, split 60% train / 40% validation; do not add keywords from failed queries ("that's overfitting"). Open specification.
Skill output test: start with 2-3 cases, run with and without the skill, clean context each run, concrete assertions ("Require concrete evidence for a PASS"), drop assertions that always pass.

Three areas of skill testing: triggering (should and should not), function, and comparison with a baseline. Thresholds such as 90% triggering are "aspirational targets - rough benchmarks" with no measurement method; the numeric thresholds are an open point.

`claude plugin eval`: each case runs 3 times, default threshold 1.0, with a no-plugin baseline (WITH and W/OUT), isolated from user `CLAUDE.md` and hooks, score is indicative only. Needs v2.1.269+; early access and may be disabled server-side; it does not measure a current harness directly.
`claude plugin test` runs mod tests without a session or network; `claude plugin validate` checks structure. Mods are a new feature.

Use an independent reviewer that has not seen the author's reasoning: "A fresh reviewer does help, because it hasn't seen your reasoning"; "Independent review instances ... are more effective at catching subtle issues than self-review instructions or extended thinking". Whether this holds for a review role running a smaller model is an open point.
Have several agents vote before a finding is posted; measure the rate of rejected findings; reviewer changes also go through evals. Secondary source.
Many adversarial review agents can make a system too complex; review intent rather than single lines at high volume.
Red-team with documents, emails and tool output that deliberately contain injected instructions; monitor outputs.
Do not conclude from aggregate numbers; sample in strata by document type or field.
Iterate by tests: write the test first, "fix the code, not the test"; the test exists before the fix and the agent cannot edit it.
Test blocking hooks: each blocking hook has one real failing case; test that a deny rule truly blocks even when a broader allow exists; check that the sandbox is really on. Inferred.
Measure cache hits and context use (`cache_read_input_tokens`, `/context`, `/usage`) when evaluating a harness. Inferred.
Debug skill triggering by asking Claude "When would you use the [skill name] skill?" so it quotes the description back; use `claude --debug`.
A three-stage checklist (before starting, during development, before upload) can be turned into a lint. The checklist is stated, the lint is inferred; the guide is dated January 2026.
When the model changes, re-evaluate prompts on representative tasks: "compare results on representative tasks". Non-vendor source.
